title: A Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales

author.name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
author.biography: Born in Salem, Massachusetts, he published The Scarlet Letter in 1850 and turned to Greek myths for children the following year.

hook.text: What would you do if a wish came true exactly as you asked it?

paragraphs: On a misty autumn morning at Tanglewood, a country house in the hills of western Massachusetts, a crowd of children is waiting to go nutting with Eustace Bright, an eighteen-year-old college student. To pass the time he tells them a story: how young Perseus set out to bring back the head of the Gorgon Medusa.

So begins A Wonder Book, six Greek myths told to the children, with their questions and Eustace's teasing between the stories: King Midas and his golden touch, Pandora and the box she was told not to open, Hercules and the golden apples, the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon, and Bellerophon and the winged horse Pegasus.

Tanglewood Tales, the second part, gives six more, told straight through: Theseus and the Minotaur, Hercules among the Pygmies, Cadmus and the dragon's teeth, Circe's palace, Proserpina carried off underground, and Jason's voyage for the Golden Fleece.

Hawthorne changed the myths freely to make them stories for children. His Midas has a little daughter, and his Pandora is a child herself. In his preface he says he did not write down to his readers, because children feel deep and lofty things more than adults think.

orientation.text: Fourteen chapters: Hawthorne's preface, six stories, a short visit to Hawthorne's own house that introduces the second part, and six more stories. Each myth is complete in one chapter, so you can stop between them.
